value.trigger: Voted into the Hall of Fame: Y98
value.text:
Fourteen rings, eight Super Bowl MVPs, and the last carry came in a championship season.

Ryland Maxwell arrived with the Jets in Y80 as Offensive Rookie of the Year and won two titles there. He went with Dorren Skura to Atlanta, where the Falcons won five straight from Y83, then rejoined him in Philadelphia in Y91. The Eagles won seven in a row, the last in Y97, his final season, and he was Super Bowl MVP one more time to close it.

He ran for 33,955 yards on 4,133 carries over 341 games, more than anyone in league history, and scored 440 rushing touchdowns, the record on Skura's club board. The league's best rushing season is his as well: 2,839 yards in Y92.

In Y94 he caught 53 touchdown passes, still the league record for a season, and was named MVP, completing a ring, Rookie of the Year, three Offensive Player of the Year awards and a Super Bowl MVP. Nobody had run the Gauntlet before him. Mad Max, welcome to the Hall of Fame.

value.trigger: Voted into the Hall of Fame: Y98
value.text:
Forty-seven interceptions, and nobody in league history has more.

Jamon Brooker spent fifteen seasons in the Green Bay secondary, from Y83 to Y97, and arrived as Defensive Rookie of the Year. He made 2,835 tackles in 266 games, more than ten a game from the back of the defense, and in Y88 alone he made 259, the second most in any season on file.

The ball found him too. He picked off 7 passes in Y87, drew level with Damar Hobbs for the career record at 43 in Y96, then took 4 more in his final season to own it outright.

He won Defensive Player of the Year twice. He never won a ring, and the Packers never reached a Super Bowl in his years there. The voters did not hold it against him. He goes in on the first ballot, beside Ryland Maxwell. Jamon Brooker, welcome to the Hall of Fame.

value.intro: Philadelphia won again, and its two pillars signed up for one more year. The voters made a mess of the awards, the market chased the wrong Eagles, and a record fell in Cincinnati that nobody rewarded. The arguments are ours; the figures are the league's.

takes.headline: Grover Calitro Set the League Record With 43 Rushing Touchdowns and Lost Offensive Player of the Year. Indefensible.
takes.dek: Calitro: 1,904 yards and 43 scores. The winner, Alton Yeldon: 1,558 yards and 27.
body: No back in the tracked history of this league has scored 43 rushing touchdowns in a season. Siran Spector's 42 in Y89 was the mark, and Calitro went past it while carrying Cincinnati to the Super Bowl. He ran for 1,904 yards, 346 more than Alton Yeldon, and scored 16 more touchdowns. Yeldon took the trophy home to Seattle anyway.

There is no reading of the numbers that makes this vote right. Calitro was the best offensive player outside Philadelphia and arguably the best inside it too. The Bengals lost the final 40-26, and his card still costs 189. The voters will not get a cleaner chance to be correct, and they missed it.

takes.headline: Ryland Maxwell Is 4 Touchdowns Short of Second Place. At 35, He Should Be Chasing First.
takes.dek: 2,574 yards and 25 touchdowns at 34, and 421 career rushing scores to Lane McCoy's 458.
body: Nobody runs for 2,574 yards at 34. Maxwell did, playing all 21 of Philadelphia's games and collecting his seventh Super Bowl MVP and 13th ring, and then he re-signed for Y97. He owns the career rushing yards record at 32,108, and his Career Legacy of 14,903 is the highest in the league.

But the touchdown list is still open. Lane McCoy scored 458 rushing touchdowns, Siran Spector 425, Maxwell 421. That is 4 short of second place and 37 short of first, and he scored 25 last season. Second place should fall early in Y97. First is the real chase, and a back who just led the league in rushing is the last player anyone should bet against at 35.

takes.headline: Margus Leglue's MVP Corrected Last Year's Mistake: 41 Touchdowns and 1 Interception Beats 52 and 17
takes.dek: Bones Crawford threw more touchdowns. Leglue threw 16 fewer interceptions, and the voters finally weighed both.
body: Last year this column argued that Bones Crawford's interceptions should have cost him the MVP. They did not. This year they did, and the voters were right. Crawford threw for 4,339 yards and 52 touchdowns with 17 interceptions. Leglue threw for 3,803 yards and 41 touchdowns and was picked off once.

Leglue is 36, has been a Lion since Y80 as far as the record shows, has never won a ring, and had never won this award. His card went from 237 to 874, a 269% jump that still prices him like a role player. Crawford plays with the best supporting cast in football. Leglue made Detroit go by himself. That is what most valuable means.

takes.headline: Bones Crawford's Card Rose 124% in the Year He Lost the MVP. The Market Is Buying a Retirement.
takes.dek: From 8,559 to 19,210 after a season with 17 interceptions, 7 more than the year before.
body: Crawford was the Y95 MVP with 10 interceptions. In Y96 he threw 17, lost the award to a Detroit quarterback, and watched his card climb from 8,559 to 19,210. That is not a market rewarding a season. That is a market pricing in the day Ryland Maxwell and Akiem Brock, both 35 in Y97, are gone and somebody in Philadelphia has to be the face of the club.

He has 5 MVPs and 8 rings, and the Hall of Fame watch already scores him above the bar of 65. The case is real. But a quarterback whose interceptions rose by 7 is still standing behind the two best players he has ever played with, and they will not be there forever. Buyers at 19,210 are paying for the dynasty, not for the passer.

takes.headline: A.T. Hoyer Matched the Defensive Player of the Year's 237 Tackles in 3 Fewer Games
takes.dek: Abraham Jack needed 20 games for his 237. Hoyer got there in 17, with one more interception.
body: Abraham Jack is a deserving name on a trophy. He is not the most deserving one. Jack made 237 tackles and 2 interceptions across Buffalo's 20 games. A.T. Hoyer made 237 tackles and 3 interceptions in the Raiders' 17. Per game that is 13.94 tackles for Hoyer and 11.85 for Jack, and it is not close.

The voters rewarded the playoff run, not the player. Hoyer has made 2,911 career tackles without this award, and his card nearly doubling to 5,523 says the market saw what the ballot did not. Jack's own card went to 435. One of these players is a star, and it is the one who stayed home in January.

takes.headline: Jacob Proise's Card Is Up 398% on 786 Yards. Sell It Before Everyone Else Does.
takes.dek: The tight end went from 1,109 to 5,527 while the receiver beside him gained 2,096 yards and 26%.
body: Proise had a good season: 51 catches, 786 yards and 14 touchdowns in all 21 of Philadelphia's games, and his rating jumped from 84 to 93. The market treated it like a coronation, pushing his card from 1,109 to 5,527.

Now look one locker over. Calvin Wingo II caught 104 passes for 2,096 yards and 18 touchdowns on the same offense, and his card rose 26%. Proise is a fine tight end on a team built around the league's career rushing leader, and that rating bump is real. A 398% rise for half of Wingo's production is not a valuation. It is a bubble, and bubbles pop the moment the ring count stops climbing.

takes.headline: Ty Lock Threw for 68,237 Yards and the Hall of Fame Said No. The Hall Got It Right.
takes.dek: 2 rings, both with the Jets, then a Giants career from Y83 to Y95 without another.
body: Lock's first ballot came and went, and the outrage is already loud. It should not be. He threw for 68,237 yards and 627 touchdowns, and he also threw 137 interceptions. His 2 MVPs and 2 rings are real, but both rings came with the Jets, and the Giants won nothing with him from Y83 through Y95.

Measure him against the real standard. Sherman Brandson threw for 91,463 yards. Bones Crawford, whom this column called the better quarterback 3 seasons ago, already has 5 MVPs and 8 rings. Lock was very good for a very long time. The Hall exists for the players who were the best, and he never was.

takes.headline: Six Straight Titles, and the 13-4 Eagles Were the Weakest Champion of the Run
takes.dek: 4 losses, the most since Philadelphia hired Dorren Skura, and still nobody could finish the job.
body: The Eagles went 17-0 in Y95. They went 13-4 in Y96, their most losses since Skura arrived in Y88, and then won the Super Bowl 40-26 over Cincinnati for a 6th straight title anyway. That is the indictment, and it is not of Philadelphia.

Every contender saw a beatable Eagles team this year and none of them could do it in January. The Bengals had the league's record-setting runner and still lost by double digits. Now Ryland Maxwell and Akiem Brock are coming back at 35, and the rest of the league has one more year of excuses. If it cannot dethrone a club whose two pillars are a season older, it does not deserve to.

takes.headline: Jamon Brooker Just Tied the Career Interceptions Record. He Is the Best Player Without a Ring.
takes.dek: 43 interceptions, level with Hall of Famer Damar Hobbs, 2 Defensive Player of the Year awards and a first-ballot Hall of Fame vote to come.
body: Brooker made 186 tackles and 2 interceptions for Green Bay this season, which took him to 43 for his career and level with Damar Hobbs for the league record. Hobbs is in the Hall of Fame. Brooker will be too: the Y98 class voted him in on a score of 97, second only to Ryland Maxwell's perfect 100, with 2 Defensive Player of the Year awards behind it.

What he does not have is a ring, and at 33 the window is narrowing. Philadelphia hoards them. The best defender of his generation is spending his prime in the wrong building, and whoever trades for him first will be buying the last missing piece of a Hall of Fame career.

stats.label: Defensive Player of the Year awards

takes.headline: Akiem Brock Has Never Won an Individual Award, and the Hall of Fame Watch Still Clears Him
takes.dek: 8 rings, 181 games, the highest Career Legacy of any offensive lineman, and still playing at 35.
body: Offensive linemen rarely collect trophies, and Brock has never won an individual award. What he has won is 8 rings, every one of them in Philadelphia, across 181 games. His Career Legacy of 11,394 ranks first among offensive linemen, and the Hall of Fame watch scores him comfortably clear of the bar of 65.

That is the Hall doing its job before he even gets there. A trophy-count Hall would leave him waiting behind running backs and quarterbacks with shinier shelves. This one will not. He re-signed for Y97 beside Ryland Maxwell, the back he blocks for, and when the two of them do leave, they should go in together. Maxwell gets the yards. Brock is the reason there is room to get them.

value.deck: He came out of New York as the smallest piece of a trade and became the back every other back is measured against: rings in three cities, the career rushing record and, at last, the Gauntlet.

chapters.headline: A Ring in New York Before Anyone Knew His Name
body: Ryland Maxwell's first ring came in Y80, when Dorren Skura's Jets went 15-2 and beat the Seahawks 28-26 in Super Bowl CXXXIX. Maxwell was part of it and nowhere near the center of it. His card closed that season rated 62 with a C grade, and the market valued it at 7, the kind of price reserved for depth.

Y81 brought 1,284 rushing yards and no title. Y82 brought both: 1,430 yards, 17 rushing touchdowns and a second ring after a 46-8 rout of the Eagles in Super Bowl CXLI, a club he would one day call home. Through three seasons in New York he had 3,514 rushing yards in 56 games and an Offensive Rookie of the Year award on the shelf. Useful. Not yet a reason to build a franchise around him.

chapters.headline: One Star Out, Three In, and the Smallest Piece Was the Prize
body: When Skura left New York for Atlanta after Y82, the deal that went with him looked lopsided, just not the way it turned out. Malakai Sawyer went back to the Jets as an 89-rated back with a B grade, 203 games and 13,041 career rushing yards, his card priced at 1,755. Coming the other way were Maxwell, rated 65 and valued at 12, Chance Woodrum, a 74-rated defensive back valued at 70, and Kane Van Oxley, "The Ox", an S-grade receiver valued at 1,515.

Was it a risk? By the numbers that winter, Sawyer's card was worth more than a hundred times Maxwell's, and the best asset Atlanta received never played for it: in an offseason of three- and four-team trades across the league, Van Oxley was moved on to the Bears before a single Falcons game. The bet came down to Maxwell and Woodrum. Sawyer played 96 more games and won no more rings. Woodrum won 5 more. Maxwell won 11.

chapters.headline: Five Straight Titles, and the Role Player Disappeared
body: Atlanta won Super Bowl CXLII in Y83, beating the Jets and Sawyer 40-25, and did not stop winning them until Y87. Maxwell was Offensive Player of the Year in that first season, with 1,919 rushing yards and 25 touchdowns on the ground, and Super Bowl MVP the next.

The ratings followed the rings. He was rated 75 by the end of Y84, an A grade at 87 by Y86 and an S at 96 by Y87. Y85 was the season the league took notice: 2,617 rushing yards, 39 rushing touchdowns, still the season mark on Skura's record board, and a 237-yard game against the Bills, still the best rushing game on it. Another Offensive Player of the Year award came with it. By the end of the run he had 7 rings and 15,141 career rushing yards.

chapters.headline: Left Behind in Atlanta
body: Then Skura moved on to Philadelphia for Y88, and Maxwell stayed. The Eagles won Super Bowl CXLVII that season and CXLVIII the next, the coach's titles now arriving without the back who had carried his last five. In Atlanta, Maxwell kept running: 1,403 yards in Y88, 1,172 in Y89 and 1,223 in Y90, without a single catch in the last two of those seasons. No rings came.

The market did not seem to mind. In Y88, with no title to show for it, his card passed Sawyer's for the first time, 7,837 to 7,820, and by the end of Y90 he was rated 99. The best back in the league was waiting in the wrong city.

chapters.headline: From 7 to 49,485, a Season Late Every Time
body: The card told the story a season late every time. It was worth 7 at the end of Y80 and 12 on the day of the trade. It reached 112 after Y84, with two Falcons titles already won, and 1,520 after Y86. It first passed Sawyer's in Y88, at 7,837, and more than doubled in Y92 alone, from 12,722 to 29,409, the season he ran for 2,839 yards. After Y94 it stood at 39,532, and it stood at 49,485 after Y96, with another season still to come.

chapters.headline: The Reunion, the Record and the Gauntlet
body: In Y91 coach and back were together again in Philadelphia, and the titles came back with them: four seasons, four rings, starting with a 38-23 win over the Raiders in Super Bowl CL. Y92 brought 2,839 rushing yards, the best season on Skura's record board, and in Y93 Maxwell passed Lane McCoy's 24,507 career rushing yards to take the league record. Along the way the Eagles won 49 straight games, a run that only ended in Dallas in Y94.

Y94 was a season nobody had seen before. Maxwell caught 53 touchdown passes, the most in a season on Skura's board, and was named Most Valuable Player for the first time. It was the one major award he had never won. With it he became the first player to win every one of them: a ring, the MVP, Offensive Player of the Year, Super Bowl MVP and Offensive Rookie of the Year. Ryland Maxwell ran the Gauntlet.

chapters.headline: Ikarras, the Measuring Stick
body: Every great back gets measured against Rondale Ikarras, "The Prodigal Son", the Ravens legend of the Hall of Fame's inaugural class. The comparison has gone Maxwell's way. Ikarras ran for 23,178 yards in 303 games, 76.5 a game; Maxwell has 32,108 in 323, 99.4 a game. Ikarras won 9 rings to Maxwell's 13 and 4 Offensive Player of the Year awards, one more than Maxwell, but 5 Super Bowl MVPs to his 7. He never won the MVP. Maxwell won it once, and it completed the set.

stats.label: Ikarras Offensive Player of the Year awards

chapters.headline: The Numbers Through Y96
body: His career through Y96: 32,108 rushing yards, 421 rushing touchdowns and 125 more through the air in 323 games, with 13 rings and a Career Legacy of 14,903, the highest of any player in the league, and Y97 still to play.

chapters.headline: Three More Rings, First All Time, and One Last Title at 35
body: There was no argument left to settle, and he played on anyway. In Y95 he ran for 2,141 yards and won a 12th ring, playing 18 of the Eagles' 20 games after injury cost him 2, and passed Sherman Brandson for first in Career Legacy, 14,019 to 13,540. Y96, at 34, was better still: 2,574 yards and 25 rushing touchdowns in 21 games, a 13th ring after a 40-26 win over the Bengals, and a 7th Super Bowl MVP, with the career rushing record now at 32,108 yards.

Then, rather than leave on top, he re-signed with Dorren Skura and played Y97 at 35. Injury cost him 2 of the club's 20 games; he ran for 1,847 yards and won a 14th ring, 38-22 over the Colts, with an 8th Super Bowl MVP. He retired with the rushing record at 33,955 yards, and the Y98 class voted him into the Hall on the first ballot, scoring 100, the maximum.
